regions.name: Alabama
regions.summary: One person on the call (you) can agree to recording it. You don't need the others' permission, though telling them is good practice. On a call with someone in a state where everyone must agree, follow that stricter rule.

regions.notes: Applies to confidential conversations, which includes most calls and video meetings. Saying "this call is recorded" at the start, with people staying on, is commonly treated as consent.

regions.name: United Kingdom
regions.summary: You can record a call you're in for your own use without telling the others. Sharing it, or recording for work, brings in data-protection law.
regions.notes: For work, UK GDPR applies: tell people you're recording, have a lawful reason, and keep the recording only as long as you need it.

retention.why: Keeping only the transcript and notes, not the audio, keeps less personal data, which UK GDPR asks for.

regions.name: European Union (other countries)
regions.summary: Rules on recording a call you're in differ by country; the GDPR applies on top whenever recordings are used for work.
regions.notes: Using recordings for work counts as processing personal data under the GDPR: you need a lawful reason, must tell people, and should keep recordings no longer than you need them. Recording purely for yourself (household use) is outside the GDPR. Italy, Spain, the Netherlands and Ireland generally let a participant record; Belgium, Portugal, Greece and Austria are stricter. Germany and France have their own entries.

retention.why: Keeping only the transcript and notes, not the audio, keeps less personal data, which the GDPR asks for.

regions.name: Germany
regions.summary: Everyone on the call must agree before you record it. Live transcription counts too: it captures the conversation the same way.
regions.notes: Recording the private spoken word without consent is a crime in Germany, even for a participant. Using recordings for work counts as processing personal data under the GDPR: you need a lawful reason, must tell people, and should keep recordings no longer than you need them. Recording purely for yourself (household use) is outside the GDPR.

retention.why: Keeping only the transcript and notes, not the audio, keeps less personal data, which the GDPR asks for.

regions.name: France
regions.summary: Everyone on the call must agree before you record it. Live transcription counts too: it captures the conversation the same way.
regions.notes: Recording private words without the speaker's consent is a crime. Employers must also tell staff and the works council before recording calls. Using recordings for work counts as processing personal data under the GDPR: you need a lawful reason, must tell people, and should keep recordings no longer than you need them. Recording purely for yourself (household use) is outside the GDPR.

retention.why: Keeping only the transcript and notes, not the audio, keeps less personal data, which the GDPR asks for.

regions.name: Switzerland
regions.summary: Everyone on the call must agree before you record it. Live transcription counts too: it captures the conversation the same way.
regions.notes: Recording a non-public conversation you're in without the others' consent is a crime.

retention.why: Swiss data-protection law asks you to keep personal data no longer than needed.

regions.name: Australia
regions.summary: It depends on the state. In New South Wales, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania everyone generally needs to agree; Victoria, Queensland and the Northern Territory let a participant record.
regions.notes: The federal law on intercepting calls can also apply to phone calls. When people are in different states, follow the stricter rule.

regions.name: New Zealand
regions.summary: One person on the call (you) can agree to recording it. You don't need the others' permission, though telling them is good practice.
regions.notes: Businesses must also follow the Privacy Act: tell people why you're recording and keep it only as long as needed.

regions.name: Ireland

regions.notes: Using recordings for work counts as processing personal data under the GDPR: you need a lawful reason, must tell people, and should keep recordings no longer than you need them. Recording purely for yourself (household use) is outside the GDPR.

retention.why: Keeping only the transcript and notes, not the audio, keeps less personal data, which the GDPR asks for.

sources: Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) Act 1993

regions.name: India
regions.summary: There's no law that clearly allows or forbids a participant recording a call. Courts have sometimes refused secret recordings as evidence on privacy grounds.
regions.notes: For work, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act requires notice and consent for collecting personal data.
sources: Constitution of India, Art. 21 (K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017)

regions.name: Japan
regions.summary: One person on the call (you) can agree to recording it. You don't need the others' permission, though telling them is good practice.
regions.notes: Businesses must state why they collect personal information, including recordings.
sources: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI)
